Rutgers Solar Car aerobody, Ansys Fluent 2026 R1 Student, 6 runs, 25 to 26 Nov 2026

Tails B and C cut drag 18% against the Kamm tail. Build C.

Same nose, same 1600 mm width, same side profile, same physics. Only the tail changes. The pointed tails (B, C) reach a drag coefficient of 0.099, the Kamm cutoff (A) 0.121. At the 22 m/s cruise that is about 150 W less power fighting air. B and C are tied within 0.3%, so the pick between them comes down to building it: C is one straight taper with one fillet per side, B is three facets and three fillets.

All six runs converged, and the ranking holds on both meshes

Each tail was solved on a coarse mesh (about 575k cells) and a finer medium mesh (about 750k cells). If refining the mesh barely moves the answer, the answer is not an artifact of the mesh. Every tail moved less than 1%.

Cd and Cl are averages over the last 100 iterations; over those 100 iterations Cd moved by less than 0.00001 in every run. The pressure/friction split comes from Fluent's force report on the medium meshes. Negative Cl means the body is pulled toward the road (downforce).

Recommendation: tail C, with two checks before you commit

Why C over B

  • Drag is a tie. 0.0988 vs 0.0991 is 2 W, well inside what this level of simulation can resolve.
  • C is easier to make. One flat taper per side and one fillet, against B's three facets and three fillet radii. Fewer facets means fewer mould joints and simpler layup, which is the project's main goal.
  • C has the lowest pressure drag (0.0580), the part of drag set by shape. B has slightly lower skin friction because it has less surface.
  • No separation on C. Before the runs I expected its 16.8° plan taper to separate. The wall-shear plots show the flow staying attached all the way to the tip, so that worry is not borne out here.

Why not A, and what A still has

  • A loses on both parts of drag. Pressure Cd 0.0729 vs 0.058 to 0.059, friction 0.0482 vs about 0.040.
  • Its flat base is not the problem. The Kamm base itself is only Cd 0.0014 (about 1% of A's drag). A carries its full width 1300 mm further back, so it has more wetted surface and a longer, fuller rear body.
  • A has the most room inside: 3.21 m³ solid volume vs 2.35 (B) and 2.56 (C).
Check 1: packaging. Confirm the driver, battery box and chassis fit inside C's tail taper. The side profile is still a placeholder until real chassis numbers exist.
Check 2: crosswind. A pointed tail can behave worse than a Kamm tail at yaw. Run C and A at 5° and 10° yaw before final sign-off.

How to read the images

All images are real Ansys Fluent renders from the medium-mesh results. The half model was mirrored about the centerline so you see the whole car. Each view uses the same colour scale for A, B and C, so colours compare directly. Air flows from left to right in every image.

Pressure coefficient (Cp)

Red (+1): air slamming into the surface, as at the nose. Blue (−1): air speeding over a crest and pulling on the skin. Big blue zones near the tail, or a rear that never recovers toward zero, mean pressure drag.

X-wall shear stress (Pa)

How hard the air drags along the surface in the flow direction. Positive (green to red): flow attached and moving rearward. Negative (blue): flow reversed, meaning separation. This is the standard way to find separation on a body.

Velocity magnitude (m/s)

Orange is free stream (22 m/s), dark red is air sped up over the body, and blue/green is slow air. Behind the car the slow region is the wake. A thinner, shorter wake means less energy lost, which means less drag.

Pressure: same nose, the rear is where the tails differ

All three show the red stagnation zone on the nose and blue suction bands where the surface turns over a crease (nose to roof at about 1.4 m, flat to tail). Compare the rear third: on B and C the pressure climbs back toward zero over a longer taper, which pushes the car forward and offsets the nose load. That recovery is what lowers pressure drag.

Wall shear: attached flow on all three, no separation on the tails

The only blue (reversed flow) is a sliver at the very nose tip. That is the stagnation point, where flow splits, and it is normal. The tails stay green to the end, so the flow does not separate on the top or the sides. The red bands are where flow accelerates over the nose crease. Skin friction is spread over every square metre of surface, which is why the larger body (A) has more of it.

Top view

Side view

Wake: A leaves a blunt dead-air pocket, B and C a thin trail

The centerline slice cuts the car down the middle (side view). The mid-height slice cuts horizontally at 475 mm (seen from above). Behind A's flat base there is a pocket of near-zero velocity (blue). B and C close down to a narrow, faster-recovering wake. The underside also shows the air speeding up in the 150 mm ground gap (dark red), which is the source of the downforce.

Centerline slice, side view

Mid-height slice, top view

Convergence: every run flattened out well before it stopped

Cd settles within about 100 to 150 iterations and then stays flat. The runs went to 300 to 500 iterations to be sure. A curve still drifting at the end would mean the number is not final; none are.

What was done, step by step

StepWhatWhy it matters
1. GeometrySolid A/B/C parts exported from SolidWorks (STEP + Parasolid)Fluent needs a closed body; the shelled parts are open rings
2. Air boxBox 50 m long, 7 m tall, 7 m wide; 15 m of air ahead, 30 m behind; the car cut out; only half the car (split on the centerline)Walls far enough away not to squeeze the flow (1% blockage); the half model doubles the resolution you get from the Student cell limit
3. BoundariesInlet 22 m/s, outlet 0 Pa, ground moving at 22 m/s, top/side/centerline as symmetry, car as wallA moving ground is how the road really looks to the car; a fixed ground would fake a boundary layer under it
4. MeshFluent Meshing watertight workflow, poly-hexcore; 8 prism layers on the car (0.5 mm first layer, ×1.2 growth); finer boxes around the car, under it and in the wake; coarse 30 mm and medium 20 mm surface cellsPrism layers capture the thin boundary layer that sets skin friction; refinement boxes resolve the wake that sets pressure drag
5. PhysicsSteady, pressure-based coupled solver, k-omega SST turbulence, second order, air 1.225 kg/m³SST is the standard RANS model for vehicle bodies and predicts separation better than k-epsilon
6. Runs6 runs (3 tails × 2 meshes), 300 to 500 iterations, Cd logged every iteration, 4 coresTwo meshes per tail prove the ranking is not a mesh artifact
7. Post-processingForce breakdown, y+ check, 15 Fluent images on identical scalesStandard set teams use to explain why a shape wins, not just which

Confidence: trust the ranking, not the third decimal

  • Ranking: high confidence. 18% gap between A and B/C, mesh-independent within 1%, same setup everywhere.
  • B vs C: a genuine tie. A 0.3% difference is below what this setup can separate.
  • Absolute Cd: optimistic. This is the body alone, with no wheels, wheel fairings, canopy, mirrors or panel gaps. A real car will be higher. Use these numbers to compare shapes, not to quote the car's drag.
  • Student license limits. Under about 1M cells and 4 cores. The wall cells sit at y+ about 14 (average), between the two ideal ranges (about 1 for fully resolved, over 30 for wall functions). k-omega SST tolerates this, but skin friction is the least certain number here. A research license would allow y+ about 1.
  • Steady RANS. It averages the flow over time. It can under-predict separation on tapered tails, so the "no separation on C" result is worth confirming at yaw.
  • Downforce cost. Cl about −0.42 is roughly 130 N of downforce on the full car. With a typical solar-car tire rolling resistance coefficient around 0.005 (an assumption, not measured), that adds about 14 W of rolling loss, similar for all three tails. Worth shaping the underbody later.

Next steps, in order

  1. Pick C, then check packaging: driver, battery and chassis inside C's tail.
  2. Run A and C at 5° and 10° yaw (crosswind) to confirm C keeps its lead.
  3. Fillet the long top and side creases on C and rerun one case. Sharp longitudinal edges make vortices.
  4. Add wheels and wheel fairings and the canopy for a full-car number.
  5. Ask the team advisor about a Rutgers academic research license (no cell cap) for a y+ about 1 final run.
  6. Optional: an Ahmed body validation run to calibrate the setup against wind-tunnel data.
